candidates.statement: BM25 is a robust zero-shot baseline that generally outperforms many more complex approaches on BEIR, despite underperforming neural models in-domain on MS MARCO by 7-18 points.
No single retrieval architecture consistently outperforms all others across all 18 BEIR datasets.
In-domain accuracy does not predict zero-shot out-of-domain generalization; models trained on identical data generalize differently.
Cross-attentional re-ranking (BM25+CE) gives the best average zero-shot performance (+11% vs BM25), beating BM25 on 16/18 datasets, failing only on ArguAna and Touche-2020.
Late-interaction ColBERT gives the second-best average zero-shot performance (+2.5%), beating BM25 on 9/18 datasets.
DeepCT and SPARTA perform well in-domain but fail to generalize, underperforming BM25 on nearly all datasets (-27.9%, -20.3% average).
docT5query generalizes well, slightly beating BM25 on average (+1.6%) and on 11/18 datasets.
Dense bi-encoders (DPR, ANCE, TAS-B) underperform BM25 on average zero-shot; DPR (the only model not trained on MS MARCO) generalizes worst overall.
TAS-B is the best-generalizing dense retriever, beating ANCE on 14/18 and DPR on 17/18 datasets.
TAS-B's stronger generalization plausibly reflects its training setup (in-batch negatives + Margin-MSE loss + strong-teacher distillation), not architecture alone.
TAS-B underperforms ANCE specifically on TREC-COVID (17.3 pts) and Touche-2020 (7.8 pts), associated with a systematic document-length preference.

A controlled ablation changing only the similarity function (cosine vs dot-product) reproduces a length preference and a 15.3-point TREC-COVID nDCG@10 change, indicating the similarity function contributes causally to the preference.
GenQ improves over TAS-B on specialized domains but underperforms TAS-B on broad/generic domains such as Wikipedia.

The best-generalizing architectures (re-ranking, late-interaction) are also the most computationally expensive (>350ms vs <20ms for dense, 20-25ms CPU for sparse) -- a performance/efficiency trade-off.
Index-size costs scale very differently by architecture; ColBERT's multi-vector index would need ~900GB for BioASQ vs 18GB for BM25.
Several BEIR test collections (e.g. TREC-COVID) show large cross-model differences in Hole@10, indicating lexically biased annotation pools.

Manually annotating previously-unjudged hits leaves lexical methods' scores nearly unchanged but substantially raises non-lexical methods' scores, showing lexical pooling bias understates non-lexical zero-shot performance.
Robust zero-shot generalization is more closely associated with cross-attention(-like) interaction mechanisms than with the choice of dense/sparse embedding architecture alone.
To the authors' knowledge, BEIR is the first broad, zero-shot information retrieval benchmark, in contrast to narrower prior efforts (MultiReQA, KILT).
BEIR unifies 18 datasets/9 tasks into one data format and metric, released as open-source software for evaluating any retrieval model on any included (or new) dataset.
BEIR datasets are large in scale range (3.6k-15M documents) and vary widely in query/document length (3-192 / 11-635 words); only 8/19 provide training data.
Domain overlap across BEIR datasets is generally low, with higher overlap concentrated among datasets sharing a source domain.
